671.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
671.explanation: Mahavira urges Gautama, who has already taken the decisive step of renunciation, not to linger at the last stage but to hasten to completion.
671.tie_back: The kural's teaching that once a decision has been reached, delay is a harm is mirrored in this rebuke to halting when the goal is in reach.
671.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
671._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the harm of delay after resolve; the Jain goal is the 'other shore' of liberation, not a political decision.

672.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
672.explanation: Jain monastic discipline assigns each activity its proper time and forbids doing things out of season.
672.tie_back: The kural's rule that some tasks may be done slowly while others must not be delayed is a version of this principle that every act has its due time.
672.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
672._accuracy_note: Matches the timeliness principle but lacks the kural's explicit contrast between tasks to be done slowly and tasks needing speed.

673.quote_or_event: In the meeting of Kesi and Gautama, the followers of Parshvanatha (four vows) and of Mahavira (five vows) ask why two Jinas pursuing the same goal prescribed different forms of the Law. Gautama explains that the form was adapted to the people of each age, the earliest of whom could only with difficulty understand the precepts and the latest only with difficulty observe them.
673.explanation: Jain tradition holds that the same end may be reached by different prescribed means, chosen according to what will actually work for those concerned.
673.tie_back: The kural's advice to act directly where possible and otherwise to find a route that will work has a loose echo in this Jain acceptance of adapting means to circumstances.
673.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23 (Kesi and Gautama), esp. 23.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
673._accuracy_note: Next-best match only: the kural is about practical (often military) expedients, while the Jain passage concerns adapting religious rules to people's capacities.

674.quote_or_event: “One should not be complacent with a small debt, slight wound, spark of fire and slight passion, because what is small (today) may become bigger (later).”
674.explanation: The preceding verse warns that even one who has repressed all his passions may fall again, so one must not be complacent while remnants of passion remain.
674.tie_back: The kural's image of an unfinished task and a half-defeated foe as embers that grow back and destroy is matched almost exactly by this Jain warning about a spark of fire and the remnants of passion.
674.source: Saman Suttam 134 (cf. 133), English tr. on jainworld.com
674._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the image of a small remaining fire growing dangerous; the Jain target is inner passions (kasaya), not enemies or tasks. Saman Suttam is a 1974 anthology of older verses.

675.quote_or_event: “A person should decide upon fasting after taking into consideration his physical strength, stamina, faith, state of health, place and time.”
675.explanation: Jain teaching on austerity requires that a practice be undertaken only after weighing one's own capacities together with the place and the time.
675.tie_back: Like the kural's fivefold review of resources, instruments, time, act and place before acting, this verse makes a deliberate survey of capacity, place and time the precondition of an undertaking.
675.source: Saman Suttam 445 (Tapasutra), English tr. on jainworld.com
675._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit on weighing means, place and time before acting; the English rendering applies it to fasting, though the Prakrit line is phrased more generally.

676.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital.”
676.explanation: The parable treats human life as capital that can be increased, preserved or lost, and adds that, considering what is at stake, one should weigh the outcomes in one's mind.
676.tie_back: The kural's call to weigh the effort, the obstacles and the gain before acting is reflected in this Jain parable of reckoning the stakes and possible returns of a venture.
676.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14-15 (cf. 7.19) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
676._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on weighing gain and loss before acting; the parable's real subject is spiritual gain (heaven) versus loss (hell or animal birth).

677.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
677.explanation: The lecture on discipline teaches the pupil to grasp the mind of the experienced teacher and act upon it, and promises that satisfied teachers will hand on their weighty knowledge.
677.tie_back: The kural's method of learning the mind of one who knows the work from inside is closely paralleled by this Jain rule of taking on the teacher's intention before acting.
677.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.43 (cf. 1.46) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
677._accuracy_note: Strong fit on learning the knowing one's mind; the Jain context is the monastic pupil-teacher relationship rather than practical expertise in a task.

678.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned elephant who is inflamed by carnal desires, is turned from his way by a female elephant (and is captured and at last killed in battle).”
678.explanation: In the lecture on the causes of carelessness, the elephant lured and captured by a decoy female is an image of how attachment to the senses leads a soul to ruin.
678.tie_back: The Jain text knows the same decoy-elephant capture the kural uses, but turns it into a warning about the senses rather than a model of using one undertaking to win another.
678.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.89 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
678._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best match: the shared image is the decoy-captured elephant, but Jainism uses it negatively; the line is from Jacobi's bracketed summary of a repeated verse.

679.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
679.explanation: This verse, recited at the Jain rite of mutual forgiveness, makes friendship toward every being and enmity toward none a central discipline.
679.tie_back: The kural urges winning over those not yet one's friends; the Jain ideal goes further by refusing to regard anyone as a foe at all.
679.source: Saman Suttam 86, English tr. on jainworld.com
679._accuracy_note: Partial match: both value turning non-friends into friends, but the kural's motive is political advantage while the Jain verse is universal non-enmity.

680.quote_or_event: When Bharata, eldest son of Rishabha, set out to bring every realm under his rule as chakravartin, his ninety-eight younger brothers, each holding a smaller kingdom, were called on to submit. Jain tradition relates that rather than fight or bow, they became monks and gave up their kingdoms, leaving Bahubali alone to resist.
680.explanation: In the Jain universal history the weaker rulers neither wage a hopeless war nor merely submit, but renounce kingship altogether.
680.tie_back: The kural observes that small rulers, fearing for their people, will yield to a mightier power when an opening is offered; the Jain story shows lesser kings in the same position choosing renunciation instead.
680.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (life of Ṛṣabha and Bharata's conquest), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Bharata chakravarti'
680._accuracy_note: Next-best match from Jain narrative, checked only against a Wikipedia summary (not the Johnson translation); the Jain resolution is renunciation, not political submission.
